subject: Complex model, slow warmup, how to diagnose?

messages.author: 4b681bcd9d4d425d
messages.subject: Complex model, slow warmup, how to diagnose?
parts:
Hi,

I'm seeing really slow warmup; I suspect that rescaling or changing the model structure somewhere could help, but the models is fairly complex, and I'm unsure where to start.

One possibility is the "small" factors in the ODE; I rescaled them for sampling, but then un-scaled them when input to the ODE Solver; is that going to be a problem? (they are range-restricted to be positive, and are near 0 - but they should be near 0.)

Another is correlated parameters; is there a way to figure out where this is a problem? (Or what variables I may want to scale or shift that are leading to this?)

Basically, is there a how-to for this, or is the answer that there are no heuristics that have been developed?

Thanks,
David

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: Complex model, slow warmup, how to diagnose?
parts:
Hi David,

If you're looking for heuristics, I think it helps to think about models that definitely perform poorly:

1) hierarchical models with little data and a centered parameterization.
2) parameters with heavy tailed posteriors (e.g.- cauchy)
3) improper posteriors
4) wildly different parameter scales

Much of this stuff you can get clues about from either your parameterization or the first samples from adaptation.  It's just a lot of plotting...

Krzysztof

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Complex model, slow warmup, how to diagnose?
parts: Hi David,

On Fri, Dec 4, 2015 at 3:06 PM, David Manheim <davidm...@gmail.com> wrote:
Another idea; does using local variables in the model block require less sampling than having them in the transformed parameters section? (This isn't clear from the manual; I have about 20 variables that have derivatives computed when I try that, but a lot more transformed parameters output from the ODE model.)

No. There are very minor differences between declaring and defining a variable in transformed parameters or as a local variable within the model block. The differences:
- transformed parameters are checked for validity
- transformed parameters are output; local variables are not
The second point might make a difference if output is a bottleneck, but doesn't really affect Stan.

Regarding "requiring less sampling" -- I think you're misinterpreting what a Stan program does. A Stan program defines data, (constrained) parameters, and how to compute the joint probability function of the data and the parameters. Under the hood, Stan takes the constrained parameters and unconstrains them; that's changing the space and maps to -inf to inf. Stan also accounts for the change of variables and includes the Jacobians for the transforms automatically. (The program also generates a version without the Jacobians, but for NUTS, we use the one with the Jacobians.)

Conceptually, if you think of what happens at a single leapfrog step:
- the data are known
- the parameters are known (they've already been "sampled")
- all that's left to do is calculate the log probability function of the data and the parameters (unnormalized is fine)

Outside of the log probability function, NUTS then figures out how to pick the next set of parameter values. Once it does that, it does the same thing above.

The reason sampling is unaffected by the decision to put variables in transformed parameters or local variables is because the work is the same to calculate the log probability function.

Hopefully that makes some sense and helps.

On Friday, December 4, 2015 at 12:02:13 PM UTC-8, David Manheim wrote:
Hi,

I'm seeing really slow warmup; I suspect that rescaling or changing the model structure somewhere could help, but the models is fairly complex, and I'm unsure where to start.

Slow warmup isn't necessarily problematic. Can you calibrate? What do you consider "really slow" and "fairly complex"?

The natural place to start is simpler. Start with something that works and then build up. Start with simulated data under the same assumptions as your model and then move towards working with real data that don't have the same generative mechanism.

One possibility is the "small" factors in the ODE; I rescaled them for sampling, but then un-scaled them when input to the ODE Solver; is that going to be a problem? (they are range-restricted to be positive, and are near 0 - but they should be near 0.)

If you're playing with ODEs, then this adds another complication. We currently have a non-stiff solver in Stan that isn't that great with stiff problems. For now, one thing you can do is put a reject() statement within the ODE if the parameters are haywire. This would prevent it getting stuck within the ODE solver.

We're working on getting a stiff solver into Stan.

Another is correlated parameters; is there a way to figure out where this is a problem? (Or what variables I may want to scale or shift that are leading to this?)
 

Basically, is there a how-to for this, or is the answer that there are no heuristics that have been developed?
Start simple and build up. This works much, much, much better than start with the most complicated model you can conjure, then strip down to something that fits.

Thanks,
David

parts:
On Friday, December 4, 2015 at 3:35:57 PM UTC-5, David Manheim wrote:
Thanks! This is helpful... For all of these, are there resources for what types of things I can do to use the first samples / parameterization to diagnose the problems? That's kind-of what I was hoping to find, though the specific advice here is good as well.


 

For further questions...

On 1, I can add another layer in my heirarchical model for some of the parameters and use multiple years of data, which I will do eventually - but I'm worried this will make it worse if there are other problems. (I wanted to figure out the one-year case first.)

Take a look at what happens in one of the low-N hierarchical model examples and how the centered/non-centered parameterizations compare.  Then do the right one for your model.  Piling on more data/complexity is not worth it when you don't know if the model works.
On 2, If my priors are lognormal, perhaps I should use gamma instead? I thought I dealt with this, and I've avoided cauchy priors for this reason - I'm unsure how to figure this out.

lognormal is not a problem in and of itself (in fact Andrew and some other folks are recommending them over gamma(?)).  Look at the warmup samples (in rstan I think you need to set inc_warmup=TRUE) and see if the sampler is just wandering off in some direction in parameter space... this can be a lot of plotting if you have a lot of parameters...
On 3, I need to figure out whether my posterior is proper; the prior is proper, but conditional on data, conceivably it is not, right? If that's true I'm unsure I can guarantee a proper posterior.

I should have been more careful about what I wrote---sure improper posteriors are a problem but a more likely computational problem is that your priors are too weak.  As an example try to guess what appropriate priors are in a logistic regression with five coefficients:

logit(y_i) = B_0 + B_1 + B_2 + B_3 + B_4

Pick priors, simulate coefficients, and then see what the implied distribution is for y.  It's even worse with hierarchical priors.  This problem will bite you especially hard if you are also running the ODE solver (as Daniel points out).
On 4, this may be an issue - I didn't realize I wanted the scales to be similar, just thought they should be away from extreme values.

Yeah, make them all similar---there's something specific about what Stan expects, maybe -1 to 1 works best... then transform to whathever scales you need.  I think Stan is pretty robust with respect to this problem and I've only seen people have issues when they try BUGS tricks like making something constant by declaring it to be Y ~ N(0,.00000001) or having some coefficients on (0,1) and some coefficients for counts in the millions....  

Also there's nothing wrong with offering co-authorship unless you're trying to be the Hulk of modeling... Stan smash?

Krzysztof

Thanks a ton!

Right. Stan doesn't use any conjugacy information
unless the user programs the posterior marginalization
directly.

The main issues are the ones Andrew discusses in his
papers:

* does the prior allow support near zero
-- lognormal and gammas of various forms contrast with
half normals and half cauchiehere

* where is most of the probability mass
-- very fat (or improper) priors contrast with
more informative ones

* how fat are the tails
-- cauchy contrasts with normal here

* are values truncated or not
-- we recommend not truncating (using uniform bounded
priors) unless it's necessary for support in the model
(e.g., scale parameters must be poitive, binomial parameters
must be in (0, 1), covariance matrices must be positive
(semi-)definite).

- Bob
